BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: High pressure will peak over the region on Wednesday, with temperatures reaching about 10-15 degrees above normal and near daily record highs.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Scattered light rain showers in northern areas this evening, then a better chance of light rain Monday night. Mostly cloudy but dry in southern areas through Monday night.
- Continued above normal temperatures through the week with Wednesday the warmest day. Record high temperatures possible Wednesday through Saturday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A weak upper trough will bring scattered light rain showers to northern mountains tonight. A stronger Pacific trough will bring a better chance of light rain Monday night, again to northern areas. Total precipitation should stay less than .10 inch. Southern areas will be mostly cloudy but dry. Temperatures will lower slightly as the two troughs move through. Light winds through Tuesday mainly from the east through south, increasing Tuesday night.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: High pressure will peak over the region on Wednesday, with temperatures reaching about 10-15 degrees above normal and near daily record highs. Warm and dry conditions will continue through early Saturday, with little change day to day from Wednesday through Friday. High pressure will shift east by late Friday as southwest flow takes over ahead of a shift to cooler and wetter weather. An atmospheric river will impact the Pacific Northwest on Friday and into the weekend, with the upper level trough eventually moving east and bringing remnant moisture into southeast Oregon and southwest Idaho. Models diverge on when the trough will move into the region, however all favor a cool and wet pattern for Sunday into early next week. This system will also bring breezy southerly winds and a steady cooling trend beginning Sunday. Precipitation chances increase to 20-40% chance on Saturday in high terrain in northeast Oregon and the West Central Mountains in Idaho. Valley locations look to stay mostly dry through Saturday evening. Precipitation chances increase area wide by Sunday, with a 20-40% chance in valleys, and 40-60% in higher elevations north and west of the Snake River Valley. Warm southwest flow ahead of the trough passage will likely keep snow levels above 6500-7500 ft until they drop with the colder air mass moving into the region early next week.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Upper level ridging will develop over the western U.S. Wednesday and Thursday. An upper level low will approach the southwest coast of California Friday and Saturday, pushing the ridge axis over the area.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above normal temperatures and dry conditions will continue for atleast the next seven days.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Warm and quiet weather will continue on Monday. Mostly sunny conditions are expected with the exception of a few high clouds in the mid to late afternoon for the northern plains and higher terrain. Highs will be in the mid 60s to around 70 degrees, which is 10 to 15 degrees above normal for this time of year.

Models are in better agreement on the positioning of the upper level shortwave Tuesday into Wednesday. The GFS has trended more northeast, with the other models trending more southeast, meeting in the middle of what they've been showing the past couple of days. Although there will be some lift associated with the shortwave, moisture is too low when it moves through for precipitation development. At the surface, a cold front will move through mid Tuesday into early Wednesday. Winds behind the front will be breezy from the west/northwest which will allow for decent downsloping and warm temperatures Tuesday afternoon. This could lead to elevated fire weather conditions across portions of the northern plains Tuesday afternoon. Cooler (but still above-normal temperatures) will exist for Wednesday. However, these slightly cooler temperatures will be short- live as our next upper level ridge starts to build behind the shortwave.

Upper level ridging will develop over the western U.S. Wednesday and Thursday. An upper level low will approach the southwest coast of California Friday and Saturday, pushing the ridge axis over the area. Temperatures will remain above normal and dry Thursday through the weekend, with our next hope for precipitation early next week as the upper highs gets ushered out of our area.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: A strong ridge amplifying to our west will encroach on the area Thursday into the weekend. Expect a gradual warming trend Thursday and Friday, with 700-mb temperatures peaking around +5 to +7C Friday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Near to or just above average temperatures and dry conditions are expected to continue into mid-week.
- Breezier winds return today into Monday; however, fire weather conditions are not anticipated at this time.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Upper level ridging is still the dominant pattern in the short term forecast. On satellite, low to mid altitude clouds are starting to fill in for the Pacific Northwest as the upper low inches closer to the coastline. While low clouds aren't expected here, the skies over Southeast Wyoming will slowly start to become cloudy throughout the day Monday. Winds are also going to be rather breezy as well. That same system will push against our ridge and tightens the height gradient across the Intermountain West. The Craig to Casper gradient still looks to be around 45 to 47 meters for elevated wind conditions for our Wind prones. 700mb wind speeds look to be around 35 to 40 knots starting early Monday morning. With the synoptic winds from a Westerly direction there will some downsloping to potentially keep most areas warmer on Monday as well. The global model Omega fields also show a kind of mountain wave pattern that may exceed model surface winds especially in our wind prone areas along I-80 and I-25. Our in-house algorithm depicts a decent chance for elevated to potentially high winds along our wind prones. Other than that temperatures look to be in the 50's and 60's in the higher elevations west of I-25 but in the elevations to the east some areas will be in the mid to upper 60's. Chadron may actually have temperatures in the upper 50's due to upslope easterly winds over the Pine Ridge area. Overnight temperatures look to be in the 30's and 40's tonight and Monday. This is mostly due to the expected downsloping winds expected to occur over the next 36 to 48 hours.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Warm and dry weather is expected to continue for the rest of the operational forecast period. Picking up on Tuesday, we will have a little bit to talk about as a clipper system passes just to our northeast. Models are in good agreement keeping the system to our north meaning nearly all ensembles are totally dry for the forecast area. On the south side of the upper level shortwave, we can expect to see 700-mb winds creep up Tuesday morning. A surface cyclone will lead the upper level low developing over the Black Hills region Tuesday morning. By the afternoon hours, expect this feature to pull to the east, dragging the surface trough eastward away from the Laramie range, and thus pulling gusty west to northwest winds across the area into the High Plains. Most areas can expect maximum gusts in the 35 to 45 mph range, but there is a chance for high winds in the typical wind prone areas. Craig to Casper 700 and 850-mb height gradients are around 45 to 50 meters, which is just on the low side for high wind events. In house guidance now gives each of the wind prone areas about a 40% chance for high winds, so this will be one to watch. The best window is late Tuesday morning through about sunset. Very dry air will also mix through the atmosphere, producing at least elevated fire weather conditions. Despite modest cool air advection through the day, we should still see temperatures climb to about 10F above seasonal averages, generally in the 60s for the plains and mid to upper 50s in the valleys west of the Laramie range.

Wednesday will remain breezy, but gusts should be more in the 25 to 35 mph range. Northwest flow will persist aloft behind the departing shortwave trough. 700-mb temperatures in the 0 to +2C range will support highs closer to average, but still on the warm side. Wednesday will be the coolest day of the week, with upper 50s to lower 60s anticipated for the plains, and mid 50s for the valleys west of the Laramie range.

A strong ridge amplifying to our west will encroach on the area Thursday into the weekend. Expect a gradual warming trend Thursday and Friday, with 700-mb temperatures peaking around +5 to +7C Friday. High temperatures will remain about 10 to 15F above seasonal averages. The ridge is expected to flatten out a bit over the weekend. 700-mb temperatures drop slightly, and thus daytime high expectations are a few degrees cooler than Friday for Saturday and Sunday, but still warm for this time of year. Overall, it should be a pleasant weekend. Portions of Carbon, Converse, and Albany counties could be breezy, but nothing remotely unusual for this time of year. With little to no precipitation expected anywhere in the area for the next 7 days, it is tempting to look beyond the operational forecast period for some hints at a pattern change. Ensembles continue to kick the can down the road and push the potential change further out, but most are showing the longwave Pacific trough moving inland into the western CONUS by the weekend. If this occurs, the door to potential storminess may open again in the November 16 to 19 period. About 60% of ensembles show a storm system passing through our area during this period, while 40% remain mostly dry.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: The coming week looks to be mostly quiet for eastern Utah and Western Colorado with temperatures four to eight degrees above normal.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry conditions with temperatures about five above normal will continue through the work week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The coming week looks to be mostly quiet for eastern Utah and Western Colorado with temperatures four to eight degrees above normal. A weak ridge/high builds in over the Southwest extending to the northeast across the region with a zonal flow aloft to our north. A weak shortwave in that flow will brush the northern mountains Tuesday into Wednesday that could kick off a few light orographic showers/flurries, but don't expect any impacts with this system. With the zonal flow dipping south, we could see some afternoon and evening west to northwest winds gusting 20-30 mph across the northern areas. Wednesday into the weekend will see high pressure build in over the region with a return of mild weather. Models are indicating the next significant weather we'll see is a cold low dropping south off the West Coast this weekend that will pull subtropical moisture north into the region Sunday into early next week. It's too early to tell how much moisture will get caught up in this system, but current models are predicting pwats around 0.70 inches which is enough to give us a round of stronger thunderstorms, but not the deep moisture we've seen in the past few weeks that brings widespread flooding. Confidence is low this far out, so stay tuned, but it does look like this system will usher in a period of more unsettled weather next week.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: By next weekend, flow turns southwesterly and the upper ridge shifting east. A few showers could be possible along the Continental Divide next Saturday afternoon.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry and continued mild through the next severals days, with a brief cool down on Wednesday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently...very nice conditions continue across southern Colorado this afternoon, with light winds, clear skies and temperatures in the 50s and 60s. A few degrees of additional warming are expected this afternoon.

Tonight through tomorrow night...high pressure will dominate the weather across the region through tomorrow night. Dry weather, light winds and mild conditions are expected. Lows tonight will fall into the 30s for the Plains and 20s for the San Luis Valley. High temperatures Monday will warm through the 60s to near 70 degrees on the Plains. Temperatures will fall back to the 30s on the Plains tomorrow night and 20s across the San Luis Valley.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Good agreement through the extended period between the deterministic and ensemble guidance. The GFS has come more into line with the ECMWF and ensemble guidance with the mid week upper trough.

Tuesday through Saturday...overall, high pressure will continue to dominate southern Colorado through the next several days. This will keep temperatures mainly in the 60s to near 70 across the Plains, and 50s over the San Luis Valley. Overnight lows will fall into the 30s for the Plains, and 20s for the San Luis Valley. The upper trough forecast for mid week will pass well north and east, however, it will send a cold front across the Plains by Wednesday. This frontal boundary will be dry, and only bring a brief cool down Wednesday afternoon by about 5-8 degrees.
By next weekend, flow turns southwesterly and the upper ridge shifting east. A few showers could be possible along the Continental Divide next Saturday afternoon.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Models have converged on a continued dry and mild pattern continuing through at least Saturday as we remain under the influence of high pressure.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Patchy fog may develop again tonight in prone areas such as the Cache and Heber Valleys.
- Conditions remain dry and mild areawide through a majority of the week, with the next chance for precipitation arriving late this weekend.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Quiescent conditions prevail areawide tonight, as high pressure remains the dominant feature across the western US. Patchy fog development remains a concern overnight, especially for fog prone areas like the Cache Valley, though increasing high cloud cover across northern Utah tonight may delay or completely inhibit fog development.

Persistent high pressure has allowed for strengthening valley inversions and resultant valley haze over the past few days, which is expected to continue into Monday. A weak and dry shortwave trough traversing northern Utah on Tuesday will bring cooling temperatures aloft that may work to mix out some of the accumulated valley haze. High pressure quickly re-amplifies across the western US Wednesday through the latter half of the week, keeping haze in place through this period.

Models have converged on a continued dry and mild pattern continuing through at least Saturday as we remain under the influence of high pressure. The pattern becomes more progressive across the west on Sunday as a cutoff low off the coast of southern California moves inland. This system brings our first shot at precipitation, though uncertainty in the exact track of the low is leading to low confidence at this time.

2660.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Avalanche conditions are generally safe. The ony place you can trigger an avalanche are very steep upper elevation terrain features with previous wind loading. Steer around old, hard drifts of snow in consequential terrain.

2747.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe for travel and hold too little snow to produce an avalanche. At high elevations, steer around firm, drifted snow features if you find them below ridges or in deeper gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

(Precipitation data are recorded from Secesh SNOTEL site at 6540')

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: Most slopes are generally safe for travel. Previous wind-drifted slopes at higher elevations on the north half of the compass are lingering places where you could trigger a small slide. Look for stiffer snow surfaces or rounded drifts below ridges or deeper gullies as features to avoid, especially in steep, consequential terrain.
